documents.title: Process Management and Scheduling
documents.text: An operating system manages the execution of processes. A process is a program in execution, consisting of the program code, current activity, program counter, registers, and memory stack. The process lifecycle transitions through states: New, Ready, Running, Waiting, and Terminated. The CPU scheduler selects among ready processes using algorithms such as First-Come First-Served (FCFS), Shortest Job First (SJF), Priority Scheduling, and Round Robin (RR). Preemptive scheduling allows the operating system to interrupt a currently running process when a higher-priority process arrives or when its time quantum expires. Non-preemptive scheduling lets a process hold the CPU until it terminates or voluntarily switches to a waiting state. documents.title: Concurrency, Deadlocks, and Synchronization
documents.text: A deadlock is a situation where two or more competing processes are unable to proceed because each is waiting for a resource held by another. Four Coffman conditions must hold simultaneously for a deadlock to occur: Mutual Exclusion, Hold and Wait, No Preemption, and Circular Wait. If any one of these conditions is prevented, deadlock cannot occur. Deadlock handling strategies include avoidance, detection, prevention, and ignorance (the Ostrich algorithm). Dijkstra's Banker's algorithm is a classic deadlock avoidance method that ensures the system remains in a safe state by simulating resource allocation before granting requests. Process synchronization coordinates concurrent execution using primitives such as semaphores, mutexes, and condition variables. A mutex provides mutual exclusion using binary ownership, whereas a semaphore maintains an integer counter signaling resource availability.

documents.title: Virtual Memory and Paging
documents.text: Virtual memory provides an idealized, uniform address space to processes, abstracting physical RAM. The Memory Management Unit (MMU) translates virtual addresses into physical addresses using page tables. In a paging system, physical memory is partitioned into fixed-size frames, and virtual address space is divided into equal-sized pages. A Translation Lookaside Buffer (TLB) acts as a fast associative hardware cache for virtual-to-physical address translations. When a process accesses a page not present in physical RAM, the hardware triggers a page fault trap, causing the OS to fetch the missing page from secondary storage. Page replacement algorithms determine which frame to evict, including Least Recently Used (LRU), First-In First-Out (FIFO), and Optimal (OPT). Excessive paging activity where the system spends more time swapping pages than executing instructions is termed thrashing.

documents.title: Relational Model and ACID Properties
documents.text: Relational database management systems (RDBMS) organize data into structured tables with rows (tuples) and columns (attributes). Relational integrity is enforced using primary keys and foreign keys. A transaction is a logical unit of work that must satisfy ACID properties: Atomicity guarantees all operations succeed or all are rolled back; Consistency ensures the database transitions between valid states satisfying all invariants; Isolation guarantees concurrent execution yields identical state to serial execution; and Durability ensures committed updates persist even during system crashes. Concurrency control techniques include Two-Phase Locking (2PL), Multiversion Concurrency Control (MVCC), and optimistic locking. Write-Ahead Logging (WAL) guarantees durability by appending change records to persistent disk logs before data pages.

documents.title: Database Normalization and B-Tree Indexing
documents.text: Database normalization organizes relational schema to reduce data redundancy and eliminate insert, update, and delete anomalies. First Normal Form (1NF) requires atomic attribute values; Second Normal Form (2NF) eliminates partial dependencies on composite candidate keys; Third Normal Form (3NF) removes transitive dependencies. Boyce-Codd Normal Form (BCNF) strictly requires every determinant to be a superkey. Database indexes accelerate retrieval operations at the cost of additional storage and write latency. B+ Trees are balanced search trees widely used for database indexing because all values reside at the leaf level, forming a linked list optimized for sequential range scans. Clustered indexes dictate the physical sort order of table data rows on disk, meaning a table can have only one clustered index. Non-clustered indexes create separate auxiliary structures with pointers back to the base

documents.title: Transport Layer Protocols: TCP and UDP
documents.text: The transport layer provides host-to-host communication services. Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) is a connection-oriented, reliable protocol that provides ordered, byte-stream delivery with flow and congestion control. TCP establishes connections via a three-way handshake: SYN, SYN-ACK, and ACK packets. Reliability is achieved via sequence numbers, acknowledgments, sliding windows, and retransmission timeouts. Congestion control algorithms such as AIMD, Slow Start, Congestion Avoidance, and Fast Recovery adapt throughput to network capacity. User Datagram Protocol (UDP) is a connectionless, lightweight protocol without delivery guarantees or flow control. A UDP packet header has a fixed 8-byte overhead, making it ideal for real-time applications such as video streaming, DNS queries, and voice over IP (VoIP), where low latency takes precedence over complete packet delivery.

documents.title: The OSI Seven Layer Architecture
documents.text: The Open Systems Interconnection (OSI) model standardizes network communication functions across seven layers: 1. Physical layer transmits raw bit streams over physical media. 2. Data Link layer handles node-to-node frame delivery and MAC addressing (Ethernet, switches). 3. Network layer handles logical IP addressing and packet routing across networks (Routers, IPv4, IPv6). 4. Transport layer provides end-to-end communication, segmentation, and reliability (TCP, UDP). 5. Session layer manages dialogue control and session checkpoints. 6. Presentation layer handles data formatting, serialization, compression, and encryption (TLS, JSON). 7. Application layer interfaces with user software services (HTTP, SMTP, SSH, FTP). Each layer encapsulates data from the layer above by prepending header information.

documents.title: Trees, Graphs, and Asymptotic Complexity
documents.text: Trees and graphs are fundamental non-linear data structures. A Binary Search Tree (BST) maintains the property that the left subtree contains keys smaller than the node, and the right subtree contains keys greater. Balanced BSTs such as AVL trees and Red-Black trees guarantee O(log n) time complexity for search, insertion, and deletion by performing rotations during updates. Graphs consist of vertices (nodes) and edges connecting them. Graph traversals include Breadth-First Search (BFS), which explores neighbor nodes level by level using a FIFO queue in O(V + E) time, and Depth-First Search (DFS), which explores branches deeply using recursion or a LIFO stack. documents.title: Sorting Algorithms and Computational Complexity
documents.text: Sorting algorithms arrange elements in a specified order. Comparison-based sorting algorithms have a theoretical lower bound of Omega(n log n) comparisons in the worst case. Quick Sort is an in-place divide-and-conquer algorithm that selects a pivot element and partitions the array into sub-arrays of elements smaller and greater than the pivot. Quick Sort has an average time complexity of O(n log n), but degrades to O(n^2) worst-case when unbalanced pivots are selected. Merge Sort divides the array into halves, recursively sorts them, and merges the sorted sub-arrays, guaranteeing O(n log n) time in all cases with O(n) auxiliary space. Heap Sort utilizes a binary heap data structure to achieve O(n log n) worst-case time in-place. Bubble Sort, Insertion Sort, and Selection Sort operate in O(n^2) time.

documents.title: CPU Pipelining and Cache Hierarchies
documents.text: Instruction pipelining improves processor throughput by overlapping the execution phases of consecutive instructions. The classic RISC pipeline consists of five stages: Instruction Fetch (IF), Instruction Decode and Register Read (ID), Execute (EX), Memory Access (MEM), and Write Back (WB). Pipeline hazards impede instruction throughput: structural hazards arise when hardware resources are contested; data hazards occur when instructions depend on uncommitted outputs (mitigated by data forwarding and out-of-order execution); and control hazards arise from branch instructions (mitigated by branch prediction). Cache hierarchies exploit temporal locality (recently accessed data is accessed again) and spatial locality (contiguous memory words are accessed together) to bridge the CPU-DRAM speed gap, structured across L1, L2, and L3 cache levels.

documents.title: Cryptography and Common Vulnerabilities
documents.text: Cryptography secures communication in the presence of adversarial third parties. Symmetric encryption uses the identical secret key for encryption and decryption (AES, DES, ChaCha20), providing high throughput. Asymmetric encryption employs key pairs: a public key for encryption and a private key for decryption (RSA, ECC). Digital signatures ensure authenticity and non-repudiation using cryptographic hash functions (SHA-256). Common software vulnerabilities include buffer overflows, where program input exceeds buffer bounds, overwriting adjacent stack memory and return addresses; SQL injection, where malicious SQL commands are injected into input fields bypassing authentication or exfiltrating data; and Cross-Site Scripting (XSS), injecting client-side scripts into web pages. Defensive countermeasures include input sanitization, parameterized prepared statements, Address Space Layout Randomization (ASLR), and stack canaries.
